title: Critical Language Awareness

pts: Language teaching inevitably carries ideological content — which variety is 'standard,' whose culture is centred, whose voice is authoritative.
Critical Discourse Analysis studies how language use reproduces or challenges social power relations.
This extends Unit 24's intercultural competence work into genuinely critical, rather than descriptive, territory.

v: Two short news reports of the same event, written for this book

items: Give pairs two short reports of the same event, differing in their choice of words and grammar.
Learners underline who is named as doing things and who has things done to them.
They note word choices that carry judgement, such as protesters versus rioters.
They note passive sentences that hide the agent (Shots were fired).
Groups discuss how each report positions the reader, and write a neutral version.
Compare an English report with a Kannada or Hindi one on the same event.
Support: provide a checklist of three questions: Who acts? Who is acted upon? Which words judge?
Challenge: learners analyse a real editorial of their choice and present their findings.

lines: Police clear encroachers from lake bed
Families evicted from homes near lake
T: Who are the people in the first headline?
S1: ‘Encroachers’. It sounds like they are doing something wrong.
S2: In the second they are ‘families’. We feel sorry for them.
T: Both refer to the same people. What choice has each writer made?

blocks.x: Critical Discourse Analysis studies how such choices present one view as natural (Fairclough 1989).

body: Purpose: to show how wording frames an event. Content: one photograph of a scene placed in two different frames, each labelled with a different headline, with key words highlighted. Style: clean, journalistic. Board version: two headlines side by side with loaded words circled.

items: Google News (free) for comparing coverage of one event across publications.

blocks.x: Two newspapers from the same day, with reports cut out and compared.

pts: The idea of a single 'correct' standard variety is itself a social construction, not a linguistically neutral fact.
This connects directly to Unit 24's World Englishes preview — non-standard varieties are linguistically systematic, not deficient.
Teaching a standard variety for practical, communicative reasons doesn't require treating other varieties as inferior.
points.who: Rosina Lippi-Green's work on standard language ideology

v: A set of sentences showing regional features of English

items: Show sentences with features found in Indian, Nigerian, Singaporean and other Englishes (see model language).
Learners decide in pairs whether each is ‘wrong’, ‘different’, or ‘depends on the situation’.
Discuss what makes a form ‘correct’: rules, users, context or power?
Introduce the idea of a teaching standard: a variety chosen for practical reasons, not because others are inferior.
Learners write a short paragraph explaining when they would use a local form and when a more widely understood one.
In a teacher education session, discuss how you mark local features in learners’ writing.
Support: fewer sentences, each with a short explanation.
Challenge: learners research one feature of Indian English and present its history.

lines: Please do the needful. (common in Indian English, especially in office correspondence)
He is having two brothers. (stative verb in the progressive, a well-documented Indian English feature)
She’s not coming, is it? (invariant question tag, found in several Englishes)
S: But our teacher always marks ‘is having’ wrong.
T: In an exam that expects a standard British or American form, it will be marked. That is a practical reason to learn the other form. It is not a reason to call Indian English broken.

blocks.x: Teaching a standard for communication across contexts does not require treating other varieties as inferior (Lippi-Green 2012; Kachru 1983).

body: Purpose: to show varieties as linguistically equal. Content: a circle of speakers, each with a speech bubble in their own variety, joined to a central space labelled ‘mutual intelligibility’. Style: warm, diverse, respectful. Board version: several circles joined to a centre.

items: International Dialects of English Archive (free) for recordings of different varieties [VERIFY current access].

blocks.x: Teacher reads aloud short examples; learners bring examples from films, family and the media.

body: Features such as the progressive with stative verbs and invariant question tags have been described in research on Indian English for decades. They are regular and rule-governed: features of a variety, not random errors.

pts: Native-speakerism is the often-unexamined assumption that native speakers are inherently better language teachers or models.
This bias affects hiring practices, materials design, and learner self-perception, independent of actual teaching quality or competence.
Naming it explicitly is a first step toward evaluating teaching quality on its actual merits.

v: Five job advertisements for English teachers (collected or written for the session)

items: Read the advertisements and highlight any requirement related to being a ‘native speaker’ or to accent.
Discuss what these requirements assume about good teaching.
List the qualities that actually predict good English teaching.
Rewrite one advertisement using those qualities.
Reflect on how native-speakerism may affect your own confidence, and your learners’.
Audit the audio in your coursebook: whose accents are heard, and in which roles?
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An advertisement (written for this book) and a rewrite:

lines: Original: Native speaker required. Neutral accent preferred.
Rewrite: Proficient user of English (C1 or above); teaching qualification; experience with multilingual learners; clear, intelligible pronunciation.

blocks.x: Native-speakerism is an ideology that often goes unnoticed (Holliday 2006). Teachers who share their learners’ languages and learning histories bring strengths of their own (Medgyes 1992). Unit 96 examines the native speaker idea in depth.

body: Purpose: to separate teaching quality from speaker status. Content: a set of scales; on one pan, cards labelled ‘knowledge’, ‘skill’, ‘care’, ‘language awareness’; on the other, a single small card labelled ‘birthplace’, which weighs almost nothing. Style: clear, gently ironic. Board version: two lists, one long and one with a single item.

items: TEFL Equity Advocates (free website) for resources on native-speakerism [VERIFY current availability].

blocks.x: Advertisements cut from newspapers or written on cards.

pts: Extending Unit 24's materials audit, examine explicitly whose cultural perspectives coursebooks and materials centre — and whose they omit.
This is particularly relevant in global coursebooks designed for a broad, often implicitly Western-centred market.
A critical audit doesn't demand rejecting such materials outright, but using them with conscious awareness and supplementation.

v: Teacher activity; B1–C1 learners for step 5
One unit from a global coursebook and one from a state textbook

items: For each unit, list the people shown or named: their names, places, jobs and activities.
Note whose everyday life is presented as normal, and whose appears as exotic or absent.
Note which cultures appear only as festivals, food or tourism.
Plan one supplementary text or task to widen the perspective.
Optionally, ask learners to audit a unit themselves and suggest additions.
Extend the audit to gender, rural life and disability.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: One teacher’s audit of a global coursebook unit on ‘Weekends’ (written for this book):

lines: Characters: Emma (London), Jake (Sydney), Carlos (Madrid).
Activities: skiing, brunch, shopping at a mall.
Absent: family obligations, agricultural work, weekends that include school or tuition.
Supplement: learners interview a relative about a typical weekend and write a profile; the class compares profiles with the coursebook.

blocks.x: A critical audit extends the materials audit of Unit 24. It does not require discarding the coursebook, but using it with awareness and adding what it leaves out.

body: Purpose: to show materials as windows on other worlds and mirrors of learners’ own. Content: a coursebook page drawn as a window showing distant scenes, beside a mirror reflecting a classroom of Indian learners; a pencil adds a new page between them. Style: warm, reflective. Board version: two rectangles labelled ‘window’ and ‘mirror’.

items: Google Sheets (free) for tallying representation across units.

blocks.x: A tally chart in the teaching journal.

pts: English proficiency often functions as a gatekeeper to education, employment and mobility, unevenly distributed by socioeconomic access.
This context shapes what English teaching means for different learners in different circumstances, beyond the classroom itself.
Awareness of this doesn't change classroom technique directly, but it should inform a teacher's larger professional perspective.

v: Chart paper; short case descriptions written for this book

items: Learners map where English is needed in their community: which jobs, courses, offices, websites.
Read four short cases of young people with different access to English (see model language).
Groups discuss what English opens and closes for each person.
Learners write a short reflective paragraph on English in their own future.
In a teacher education session, map English access across schools in one district.
Support: provide sentence starters (‘English helps… because…’; ‘Without English…’).
Challenge: learners compare the role of English with that of their home language in the same situations.

lines: Kavya, Bengaluru: English-medium private school; English at home with parents.
Ravi, a village near Raichur: Kannada-medium government school; first English conversations at an engineering college.
Sana, Hyderabad: Urdu and Telugu at home; English-medium school; worries about her accent.
Joseph, Kochi: Malayalam-medium school; works in a hotel and learnt English on the job.

blocks.x: English often acts as a gatekeeper to education and employment, and access is uneven (Ramanathan 2005). This awareness shapes a teacher’s sense of what is at stake for each learner.

body: Purpose: to show English as a gatekeeper. Content: gates labelled ‘college’, ‘jobs’ and ‘online information’; learners arrive with keys of different sizes, some with none. Style: symbolic, respectful. Board version: a row of gates with arrows.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for a shared map of where English is used.

blocks.x: A hand-drawn map of the town or village on chart paper.

points.sub: More than a skill being acquired
pts: Learning a new language can involve renegotiating aspects of identity, especially for learners in prolonged immersion contexts.
This connects to Unit 22's affective factors — identity-related anxiety is a distinct dimension worth teacher awareness.
This isn't a call for informal psychoanalysis, simply informed sensitivity to a real, sometimes under-recognised dimension of learning.

items: Learners draw a language portrait: an outline of a body, coloured to show the languages in their life and where they feel them.
In pairs, they explain their portrait, in English or with support from the home language.
Learners write a short reflection: When do I feel like myself in English? When do I not?
The teacher reads reflections privately and responds with brief, supportive comments.
Use insights to adjust the classroom climate (Unit 22), not to diagnose individuals.
Older learners write a short language autobiography instead of drawing.
Support: a word bank of feelings and places.
Challenge: learners compare their portrait with a partner’s and discuss differences.

blocks.x: A learner’s reflection (written for this book):

lines: Kannada is in my heart because it is my mother’s language. Hindi is in my ears from films. English is in my hands, because I write it, but not yet in my mouth. When I speak English in class I feel like someone else.
T: Thank you. Many people feel that. What might help English come ‘into your mouth’?

blocks.x: Learning a language can involve renegotiating identity, and this affects learners’ investment in speaking (Norton 2013). The teacher’s role is informed sensitivity, not counselling.

body: Purpose: to show languages as part of identity. Content: an outline of a young person coloured in several colours, with a key naming Kannada, Hindi, English and Urdu, and small labels such as ‘heart’, ‘ears’ and ‘hands’. Style: hand-drawn, warm. Board version: a simple outline with coloured areas.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable body-outline template.

blocks.x: A body outline drawn on the board for learners to copy.

pts: Critical awareness doesn't require abandoning existing methodology — it means using it with conscious, reflective purpose.
Small, practical steps: diversifying materials' cultural representation, discussing language variety non-judgementally, examining one's own assumptions.
This connects to Unit 25's principled eclecticism — critical awareness is one more informed lens applied to every methodological choice.

items: Choose one unit you will teach this term.
Plan three small steps: one to diversify representation, one to discuss language variety without judgement, and one to examine your own assumptions.
Teach the unit as planned, adding the three steps.
Note learners’ responses.
Share what happened with a colleague and decide which step to keep.
Plan the steps with a colleague who teaches the same grade.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Three steps for a Class 11 unit on travel writing (written for this book):

lines: Representation: add an extract of travel writing by an Indian writer alongside the textbook’s British one.
Variety: a ten-minute discussion of words Indian English has given to world English (‘bungalow’, ‘jungle’, ‘shampoo’).
Assumptions: notice whether I praise learners with ‘good accents’ more readily, and adjust.

blocks.x: Critical awareness does not replace methodology; it adds a reflective purpose to it, in the spirit of the principled eclecticism of Unit 25 and Freire’s (1970) view of education as a practice of freedom.

body: Purpose: to show critical pedagogy as practical. Content: three stepping stones across a stream, labelled ‘representation’, ‘variety’ and ‘assumptions’, with a teacher crossing. Style: gentle, encouraging. Board version: three circles in a line with labels.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared list of supplementary texts by diverse writers.

blocks.x: A class library shelf of stories and articles from Indian and other writers.

pts: Critical language awareness aims to inform practice with honesty about power and inequality, not to undermine the value of language teaching itself.
Most working teachers operate within institutional and market constraints they didn't create and can't unilaterally change.
The realistic goal is conscious, reflective practice within real constraints — not an impossible demand for ideological purity.

v: Teachers; DIET or teacher education groups

items: Give groups four scenarios that involve a tension between critical awareness and institutional reality.
For each, list what is within the teacher’s control, what is partly within it, and what is outside it.
Agree one realistic action for each scenario.
Discuss: what would an unrealistic demand for ‘ideological purity’ look like here?
Each teacher writes one commitment for the next term.
Trainees role-play a talk with a parent who wants only ‘British English’ taught.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A scenario and one group’s response (written for this book):

lines: Scenario: the school uses a global coursebook it cannot change; the board exam expects a standard form.
Within control: supplementary texts; how local forms are discussed; tone of feedback.
Partly within control: choice of reading for the school library; suggestions to the department.
Outside control: board syllabus; exam format.
Action: teach the expected standard clearly, explain why, and never describe learners’ English as ‘wrong English’ when it is simply local.

blocks.x: Most teachers work within constraints they did not create. The realistic goal is conscious, reflective practice, not purity.

body: Purpose: to show realistic action within constraints. Content: three concentric circles labelled ‘within my control’, ‘within my influence’ and ‘outside my control’, with examples placed in each. Style: clear. Board version: three circles with lists.

items: Mentimeter (free plan, limited questions) to collect commitments anonymously.

blocks.x: Commitments written on slips and kept in an envelope for review at the end of term.

body: Choose one unit you will teach next month. Audit it for whose voices and varieties it centres, add one supplementary text or discussion, and note how learners respond. Share one finding at your next department or cluster meeting.

dek: Unit 59 of 100: closing this stretch of deep dives by examining the power, ideology and inequality embedded in language teaching — not just its linguistic content.

aims.x: The units so far have treated English mainly as a system to be taught well. This unit asks a different kind of question: whose English, whose culture, and whose voice does our teaching centre, and with what consequences? Critical language awareness examines the power, ideology and inequality that run through language and language teaching. The aim is not cynicism but teaching with open eyes, especially in India, where English carries great prestige and is unequally available.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain how language use can reproduce or challenge relations of power, drawing on Critical Discourse Analysis;
describe standard language ideology and distinguish a teaching standard from a judgement of worth;
recognize native-speakerism in hiring, materials and learners’ self-perceptions;
audit teaching materials for whose cultures and perspectives they centre and omit;
discuss English as a gatekeeper to opportunity in the Indian context;
respond sensitively to identity-related dimensions of language learning;
take small, practical steps towards critical pedagogy within an ordinary syllabus;
keep a balanced, realistic view of what critical awareness can and cannot change.

why: Why this matters. Teaching English is never a neutral technical act. Whose English, whose norms, and whose voices are centred are pedagogical choices with real consequences.

background.x: Norman Fairclough (1989) argued that language is a social practice bound up with power: the way institutions speak and write both reflects and helps maintain social relations. His Critical Discourse Analysis asks who is named as acting, who is acted upon, and what is presented as common sense. In a collection titled Critical Language Awareness, Fairclough (1992) and his colleagues argued that language education should help learners notice these patterns, not only master forms.

Rosina Lippi-Green (2012) described standard language ideology: the belief that one variety, usually the one used by powerful groups in writing, is inherently correct and that others are deficient. Linguistically, all varieties are systematic. Adrian Holliday (2006) named native-speakerism, the assumption that ‘native speakers’ are the best models and teachers, and showed how it shapes professional life. Péter Medgyes (1992) had earlier argued that teachers who are not native speakers bring distinct strengths, including shared experience of learning the language. Robert Phillipson (1992) described the global spread of English in terms of linguistic imperialism, a view that later writers have debated and qualified by showing how teachers and learners reshape English for their own purposes. Bonny Norton (2013) showed how identity and power shape learners’ investment in a new language. Paulo Freire’s (1970) critical pedagogy, which treats learners as people who read the world as well as the word, lies behind much of this work.

In India these questions are close to home. English is a language of higher education, law, much of business and social mobility, and it is taught in very different conditions in elite private schools and in government schools. Vaidehi Ramanathan (2005) documented the ‘English–vernacular divide’ in Gujarat, showing how access to English maps on to existing social differences. Braj Kachru (1983) described Indian English as a legitimate variety with its own norms. NEP 2020 stresses the value of mother tongues and multilingualism alongside English (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and NCF 2023 asks that learners’ languages and contexts be treated as resources (NCERT 2023). This unit links forward to Unit 71 (translanguaging), Unit 74 (World Englishes), Unit 96 (the native speaker myth) and Unit 98 (decolonizing ELT).

items: Text analysis. A short analysis of two texts on the same event, showing how word choice and grammar position the reader.
Materials audit. A representation audit of one coursebook unit, with a planned supplement.
Language portrait and reflection. For learners: a portrait and short reflection on languages and identity, responded to supportively rather than graded.
Teacher commitment. For teachers: three small steps planned, taught and reviewed, with notes on learners’ responses.
Which variety of English do you treat as the standard in your classroom, and why?
How do you respond when a learner uses an Indian English form in writing?
Whose lives are most visible in your teaching materials, and whose are missing?
How has the idea of the ‘native speaker’ affected your own confidence as a teacher of English?
Which one small step towards critical awareness is realistic for you this term?

perm: All headlines, sentences, advertisements, case cards, scenarios and learner reflections are written for this book; the people named are fictional. Real news reports or advertisements used in class should be short extracts with the source given. Screenshots of Google News, Padlet, Canva or Mentimeter require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Language portraits and reflections are personal; share them only with consent.

terms.def: An approach to studying how language use reflects, reproduces or challenges relations of power, for example by asking who is presented as acting and who as acted upon (Fairclough 1989).
Awareness of how language is used to shape views and maintain power, which language education should help learners develop (Fairclough 1992).
An approach to education that aims to help learners question social injustice and act to change it, associated with Paulo Freire (1970).

Controlling access to education, jobs or migration through requirements such as English proficiency or high-stakes test scores. In India, English often acts as a gatekeeper to higher education and employment.

A set of beliefs that come to seem natural and common sense within a society, such as the belief that only one ‘standard’ English is correct. Critical approaches ask whose interests such beliefs serve.
Learners’ commitment to learning a language, understood in relation to their identity and the social and economic value they expect the language to bring (Norton 2013).
An activity in which learners colour a body outline to show their languages and how they relate to them. It reveals the richness of learners’ linguistic repertoires (Busch 2012).
The dominance of one language, especially English, maintained through unequal structural and cultural relations that favour it over other languages (Phillipson 1992).
An ideology that treats ‘native speakers’ and their cultures as the model for English and its teaching, and so disadvantages other teachers and varieties (Holliday 2006).

The belief that one idealized, uniform variety of a language is inherently correct and superior, and that other varieties are deficient (Lippi-Green 1997). In ELT it can lead to devaluing Indian English and learners’ own speech.
